designs.title: Barley and Malt
designs.why: True line art: clean binary strokes, no specks under 10px, open negative space, 9% coverage. Serif captions at full size are crisp and will hold on a 156-160 mesh. Reads well from a distance as a botanical plate and works on both white and black tees.
designs.fix: Thicken the finest dashed hatching inside the grains and ear by about 1px so it doesn't break up when printed as white ink on the black tee.

designs.title: Vitis vinifera
designs.why: The drawing is lovely, but the tone is a 1-2px FM/diffusion dither: about 32,000 islands smaller than 10px across the grapes, leaves, bottle and glass. Dots that size will either wash out or fill in at the screen, so the bottle and grapes go to blotchy grey mud. You can't burn this as it stands.
designs.fix: Rebuild the tonal areas as engraved line hatching, or as a coarse AM halftone (about 45 lpi with a minimum dot of 3-4px), keeping the labels as solid type.

designs.title: Fermentation
designs.why: Line weights and type are printable on black, but up close it looks generated: garbled pseudo-text squiggles inside the yeast cells, bubbles in the wort drawn as broken open C-shapes, and a glitchy little box next to the Rising CO2 label. A sharp-eyed buyer of a $50 tee will notice.
designs.fix: Redraw the yeast-cell interiors and the fermenter bubbles as clean closed circles, and remove the glitch artefacts around the left-side labels.

designs.title: Oak Barrel
designs.why: Cleanest technical drawing in the set: even line weights, open space, no specks, dimension lines and arrowheads will hold as white ink on black. It reads as a real cooper's sheet.
designs.fix: Scale the small-caps spec text (stave and material notes) up about 15% and fix the uneven spacing ('75mm', 'QUANTITY'): at about 2.5mm cap height it's right at the limit for white on black.

designs.title: Pot Still
designs.why: Strong old-engraving look with a bold, legible silhouette from a distance, and the labels are solid serif. But at 18% coverage it's heavy, and the tight crosshatch mesh in the firebox, the worm-tub shadows and the still's shoulder has openings only 2-3px wide, which will plug and print as solid blobs.
designs.fix: Open up the crosshatch in the shadow areas (wider spacing or parallel hatching instead of tight mesh) so the gaps are at least 4px.

designs.title: Joiner's Tools
designs.why: Bold catalogue engraving with confident outlines and parallel hatching, and big, crisp serif numbering. It's trouble-free to separate and print, and reads well on the tee.
designs.fix: Correct the mallet caption glyph ('HEAD 2•½ IN.' should be '2½ IN.') and check the fraction glyphs across the sheet.

designs.title: Shaping
designs.why: This is a photo-like render converted to a 1px dither (about 37,000 specks under 10px, 26% coverage) with no line structure. At full size the hands, face and tools dissolve into noise. On press it will either fill in to mud or drop out, and it doesn't read as a designed one-ink illustration.
designs.fix: If it's kept at all, redraw it as true line art (engraved contour and hatching with a minimum stroke of 3px) and drop the dithered tones entirely.

designs.title: Motorcycle
designs.why: Good workshop-sheet layout. The monospace specs and dimension type are clean and legible, lines are solid, and it will print fine as white on black. The bike itself looks auto-traced in the engine and frame area, with blobby fills and stray broken strokes.
designs.fix: Hand-clean the main bike drawing (engine, frame and rear wheel): replace the blobby traced fills with crisp outlines and remove stray fragments.
